extraction.coverage: Read all 4038 lines of the text in six chunks: front matter, abstract, intro, theory, data, method, results, threats, conclusion, references, and supplementary S2-S48. extraction.research_question: Have gender gaps in parliamentary debating style, measured against gender stereotypes, narrowed in the UK House of Commons since 1997, and are women moving toward agentic styles over time (p.2-3, p.12)?
extraction.theory: Gender role and role congruity theory (Eagly and Karau 2002): stereotypes produce conformity through internalised standards and social sanctions. Stereotypes are dynamic (Diekman and Eagly 2000): changing social roles, public attitudes and women's rising parliamentary presence should weaken conformity pressure (p.9-13). Rival feminist institutionalism predicts women move toward communal styles as their numbers and power grow (p.13, p.26-28). The authors do not separate the mechanisms (p.12, p.29).
extraction.data: UK House of Commons debate speeches, May 1997 to March 2019 (source not named in text). Unit: one MP's speech-document per debate. Sample: 14,864 debates, 1,422 MPs (370 female, 1,052 male), 418,147 MP-debate observations (p.14-15); nearly half a million speeches (p.4). 20 parliamentary sessions, about 635 MPs per session, each MP in about 9 sessions on average (p.20). Speeches under 50 words, the Speaker's contributions and debates with fewer than five participants are dropped (p.15).
extraction.method: Eight style measures from text. Six use word-embedding expanded seed dictionaries (GloVe, 150 dimensions, window 3; sigmoid rescaling a=40, c=0.35; TF-IDF weighted sentence scores) (p.15-17, S2-S7). Complexity uses rescaled Flesch-Kincaid. Repetition uses Lempel-Ziv compression ratio. Measures standardised to mean 0, SD 1. Outcome model: Bayesian dynamic hierarchical normal model in Stan, one fit per style (three chains, 500 iterations after 250 burn-in); MP-by-session intercepts, debate random effects, random-walk priors on male baseline and female gap across sessions (p.19-22).
extraction.identification: Observational design, no causal identification strategy. Gender gaps are identified from within-debate variation because debate random effects absorb topic and debate differences (p.22-23). Robustness checks: covariate model (S20-S24), debate-type models (S25-S29), within-MP versus replacement decomposition (S30-S35), topic confounding with correlated topic models K=10 to 80 (S36-S43), and a participation test (S44-S46).
extraction.scope: UK House of Commons floor debate, 1997-2019. Population is MPs who speak in debates with five or more participants. Not campaign speech, votes, or voter sanctions. Covers the post-1997 era through 2019, with women rising from 18% to 32% of seats (p.11-12).
extraction.measures: Eight styles (Table 1, p.9). Communal: human narrative, affect, positive emotion. Agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression, negative emotion. Human validation of text scores against coder judgements (two coders, about 70 comparisons per style): correlations about 0.61 to 0.85 (Table S4, p.S17). Dictionary benchmark correlations are lower, e.g. positive emotion 0.38 and 0.34 against 0.70 and 0.71 for the embedding measure (p.S19).
key_findings: Early period: female MPs use more human narrative, affect and positive emotion, while men use more aggression and complexity, at least before 2010 (p.23-24).
Fact, repetition and negative emotion run against stereotype: women use them more than men for much of the period (p.23-24).
Six of eight styles: MP gender explains less between-MP variation in style at the end of the period than at the start (p.4).
For styles that converge, the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls by between 29% and 60% comparing periods before and after 2007 (p.25).
Fact and negative emotion diverge: gender explains about 0.6% and 2% of variation in 1997-2007, rising to about 4% and 9% after 2007 (p.25).
Aggression, complexity, affect and positive emotion gaps shrink to no consistent difference in recent years; the repetition gap stays relatively stable (p.23-26).
Change is concentrated among women: their communal styles decline while their negative emotion, fact and aggression rise, and men stay relatively stable on those (p.26-27).
Within-MP versus replacement: neither mechanism alone explains the convergence; divergence in negative emotion is almost entirely differential replacement of MPs (p.28; S30-S35).
Validation: text measures outperform standard dictionaries against human codings for every style except fact (p.S17-S19).
Covariate model (party, government status, frontbench, committee chair, age, margin, degree, occupation) leaves the main trends intact; aggression and complexity attenuate (p.28; S21-S22).
Topic confounding: a style gap on a topic largely does not predict that topic's growth; results hold for 10 to 80 topics (p.28; S40-S43).
Participation: an MP's average style does not predict how many speeches they make, so selection into debate does not drive the trends (p.28-29; S44-S45).
limitations: Voter sanctions for counter-stereotypic behaviour are not measured, so the mechanism linking debate style to voter penalties is untested (p.29-30).
Mechanisms are not separated: the authors do not disentangle the three pathways they outline (p.12, p.29).
Only legislative debate is studied; campaign communication, where voter penalties may bite harder, is not examined (p.31).
Seed dictionaries for aggression and human narrative were built by the authors from close reading (p.15).
Repetition is validated only at sentence level, which the authors concede is less suited to that concept (S18 note 3).
Complexity gap shift between 2008 and 2013 is confounded by covariates, and aggression and complexity trends attenuate (p.28; S21-S22).
Flesch-Kincaid chosen over domain-specific complexity measures for simplicity (p.17-18).
Sampler run is short (three chains, 500 iterations after 250 burn-in) (p.22).
Number of topics K is not fixed a priori; results rely on the sweep 10 to 80 (S41).

summary_md: Hargrave and Blumenau (UCL working paper; the text is dated October 2021, filed here as 2022) track how gendered debating style changed in the UK House of Commons between May 1997 and March 2019. The corpus is 418,147 MP-debate observations: 1,422 MPs across 14,864 debates. They score eight styles. Three are communal: human narrative, affect and positive emotion. Five are agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression and negative emotion. Six of the measures come from seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe embeddings, and these beat standard dictionaries against human coding for every style except fact (positive emotion about 0.70 against 0.38). Each style goes through a Bayesian dynamic hierarchical model with debate random effects, so gender gaps are estimated within debates. Early in the period, women used more communal styles and men more aggression and complexity. Women also used more fact, repetition and negative emotion, which runs against the stereotype. For six of eight styles the share of between-MP variation explained by gender fell, by 29 to 60 percent comparing the periods before and after 2007. Fact and negative emotion went the other way, rising to about 4 and 9 percent of MP-level variation after 2007. The change sits mostly with women, whose communal styles declined. The work is observational and does not separate mechanisms. For Paul's systems, the main point is that agency, communion and negative-emotion text scores can carry a gender signature that changes over time. The persona channel and affective N in the receptivity layer check for a party signature but not for gender. This is UK floor debate measured with dictionaries, not the US Congress, so any transfer is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

bearings.paper_claim: Communal styles (human narrative, affect, positive emotion) were higher among female MPs early in the period. Positive emotion and affect show no consistent significant gender gap by the latest years; the human narrative gap narrows gradually but is not stated to reach zero. For six of eight styles gender explains less between-MP style variation at the end of the period than at the start. For the converging styles the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls 29 to 60 percent comparing pre-2007 with post-2007; the converging styles are not named individually. Window: UK Commons May 1997 to March 2019. Denominator: MP-by-session variation (R2-style metric).

extraction.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
extraction.venue: NBER Working Paper 17577 (November 2011); JEL D72 D73 D78 F22 F23 J61 O31 O38
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (2,394 lines, 98,889 chars): front matter, intro, data, model, estimation, immigration section, conclusion, references, all table and figure text. Appendix Table 1 and 2 lists read as headers only. Table 2 and Appendix Table 3 layout garbled, so some coefficients partly mapped. Year hint 2014 corrected to 2011 (Nov 2011 NBER WP). Paul markup: none (n_annots 0, no annot files, no p.note). Findings capped at 12; dropped access-vs-expertise point (p.19) and Nike (fn 26).
extraction.research_question: What determines the dynamics of firm lobbying over time? Do up-front entry costs explain the persistence of lobbying status, and how do firms respond to a policy shock (the 2004 expiry of the H-1B cap expansion) at the extensive versus intensive margin?
extraction.data: Unit: firm-year. (1) Compustat panel of US-headquartered publicly traded firms, 1998-2006, balanced: 3,260 firms and 29,340 observations (Table 1; regressions use 26,080 obs per Table 2 note). Lobbying from LDA semi-annual reports via Center for Responsive Politics and Senate SOPR. Industry imports from Feenstra, Romalis, Schott (UC Davis). (2) H-1B sample: 171 major firms, 2001-2006, 1,026 obs, core 846 obs (Tables 3-4). Department of Labor LCA records (1.8 million records 2001-2006); USPTO patents and inventors with ethnicity inferred from names.
extraction.method: Reduced-form linear probability model of the lobbying indicator with lagged lobbying status and up to two lagged re-entry indicators (eq 2, p.10). Table 2: Blundell-Bond GMM (cols 2-6, lag-two instruments), OLS with state, industry and year FE (col 1), within firm-FE OLS (cols 7-8, Nickell bias acknowledged). Section 5: eq 3 interacts 2001 firm dependence (log LCA count, log Chinese and Indian patenting) with a 2004-2006 binding-cap dummy, with firm and year FE, clustered by firm. Table 4: cross-section, year FE. Table 6 uses always-lobbying firms (443 obs). Table 7 tabulates by quintile.
extraction.scope: US publicly traded, US-headquartered firms in Compustat for lobbying-participation facts (1998-2006). H-1B analysis covers 171 large patenting firms present in Compustat in all of 2001-2006 and at least 0.05 percent of US domestic patents. Era of the 65,000 cap versus the 195,000 cap (1998-2004). Excludes private firms and individual lobbyists.
extraction.theory: Dynamic entry-cost model in the tradition of Roberts and Tybout (1997): a one-time sunk cost F0 to start lobbying and re-entry costs Fj after j periods without lobbying. Continuing creates an option value, so lobbying is state dependent even after controlling for profitability (Sec 3, pp.8-10). Lobbying is a legislative subsidy and signal to politicians (Deardorff and Hall 2006), per the introduction.
extraction.identification: Persistence: state dependence in lagged lobbying status identified from within-firm variation under Blundell-Bond GMM with firm effects; authors argue lagged status proxies entry costs. Policy: the 2004 expiry of the expanded H-1B cap is treated as an exogenous natural experiment, since the expiry date was fixed years earlier and the issue was not central to firms during 2001-2003 (p.13). Test is the interaction of 2001 dependence with the post-2004 dummy plus firm and year FE. Entry (extensive margin) versus adjustment (intensive margin) comparisons in Tables 5-7.
extraction.measures: Lobbying indicator = any LDA-reported lobbying in year; high-skilled immigration lobbying = specific issues naming H-1B, L-1, PERM, high-skill bills, or the phrase high-skilled immigration (pp.5-6). Lobbying expenditure from disclosure reports (mean 475k, median 164k for active firms). Firm controls: log sales, employment, assets, R&D, lagged one year; log industry imports. Dependence: log firm LCA application count 2001; log Chinese and Indian patenting 2001 (ethnicity by name-matching commercial databases, 99 percent match rate claimed). Binding cap dummy 2004-2006.
key_findings: Few firms lobby: 10 percent of 3,260 firms lobby in at least one year 1998-2006; 6.2 percent lobby in a given year (Table 1; intro p.2).
Persistence: P(lobby this year | lobbied last year) = 92 percent, above 80 percent in almost all two-digit NAICS industries (Sec 2, p.7).

Size gradient: lobbying firms average 5,407 vs 1,423 ($m) sales and 23k vs 7k employees for non-lobbying firms (Table 1); among lobbyists, correlation with spending is 28 percent for sales and 19 percent for employment (p.7).

Entry costs: lagged lobbying raises the probability of lobbying in the current year by about 88 percent in the baseline Blundell-Bond specification (text, p.10; Table 2 values 0.84-0.88 across cols 2-6). Within-FE and some other OLS values are smaller (recovered 0.44 and 0.34), but still significant per the text (p.12).
Concentration: in a typical year 96 percent of lobbying expenditure came from firms that lobbied the previous year (p.7).
Election timing: entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year; exit is unrelated to the cycle (p.7).
Policy shock: share of firms lobbying for immigration rose from 6 to 12 percent between 2003 and 2004, tracking the ratio of H-1B issuances to the cap (Fig 5, p.16).

Dependence response (Table 5): LCA-based dependence x binding cap = 0.043 (SE 0.014) for high-skill lobbying; patenting-based = 0.029 (SE 0.012). Text: 10 percent higher foreign-worker dependence raises high-skill lobbying probability by about 0.3 to 0.4 percent (p.17).

No extensive-margin response: overall any-issue lobbying coefficients near zero (-0.008 SE 0.009; -0.019 SE 0.014, column mapping inferred). Panel E of Table 7 shows 0.00 entry for the most dependent firms that had not lobbied in 2001-2003 under both measures.

Intensive margin (Table 6, 443 always-lobbying firm-years): above-median-spending firms show elasticity 0.042 (SE 0.021) LCA and 0.033 (SE 0.022) patenting; interaction terms have t-statistics under 0.5 (p.18).

Table 7 Panel D: share of most-dependent firms lobbying for high-skill immigration in 2004-2006 is 0.48 (LCA) and 0.50 (patenting) among firms that lobbied in 2001-2003, vs 0.28 and 0.27 in Panel C for 2001-2003.
Falsification: LCA and Chinese and Indian patenting show no significant link to lobbying on Clean Air and Water, Consumer Product Safety, or Retirement (pp.15-16).
limitations: Sample is publicly traded firms in Compustat; private firms unobserved; conglomerates excluded from baseline (fn 16, p.10).
Lobbying reporting threshold of 10,000 dollars per half-year; authors argue measurement error is minimal (p.6).
Dynamic GMM with T=9 relies on lag-two instruments; Arellano-Bond results more sensitive across variants (p.12).
Within FE likely biased downward (Nickell 1981); authors present the OLS results as bounds-style checks (pp.11-12).
H-1B sample is small (171 firms, 846 core obs) and selected on Compustat coverage and patenting share (p.15); core sample is 846 not the 855 maximum (fn 25).
Dependence measured only in 2001 (predetermined); LCA counts are a demand proxy; ethnicity inferred from names, not immigration status.
Authors call the evidence suggestive in Sec 5 (p.16); topic-specific spending is not disclosed, so intensity is proxied by years listed (p.19).
Abstracts from the in-house versus outside-lobbyist choice (fn 6) and from the mechanism by which lobbying raises profits (fn 14).
Cap expiry assumed exogenous, though firms knew of it years in advance (p.13).

summary_md: Kerr, Lincoln and Mishra (NBER WP 17577, Nov 2011; the AEJ: Economic Policy version is dated 2014) study why firm lobbying is so persistent. In a balanced Compustat panel of 3,260 US-headquartered public firms, 1998-2006, only 10 percent lobby in any year and 6.2 percent in a given year. Among firms that lobbied last year, 92 percent lobby again. In a typical year, 96 percent of lobbying dollars come from firms that lobbied the year before. The authors read this as evidence of sunk entry costs in a Roberts-Tybout model. A Blundell-Bond linear probability model puts the lagged-status effect at about 0.84-0.88. Within-firm fixed-effects OLS gives about 0.44, which the authors say is biased downward (Nickell). Entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year itself, and exit does not follow the cycle. The policy test uses the 2004 lapse of the expanded H-1B cap. They interact each firm's 2001 dependence on foreign workers with a 2004-2006 dummy, with firm and year fixed effects, in 171 large patenting firms (846 core firm-years). Dependence raises lobbying on high-skill immigration (0.043, SE 0.014, LCA measure). It does not raise the chance of lobbying at all (-0.008, SE 0.009). No highly dependent non-lobbyist entered. All of the response came from firms that were already lobbying (the intensive margin). For Paul's systems this is mainly evidence about forecasting and specification. It backs Mentat's persistence-anchored lobbying forecasts, which leave out election-phase effects. It warns about the lagged-outcome lobbying equation with sector fixed effects in the sector growth study. It also shows that LDA reports cannot measure spending per issue, which is what the contested-bills question would need. The firm-level, 1998-2006 public-firm scope limits how far any of this transfers.

extraction.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
extraction.venue: arXiv 2311.16639 (v3, 5 Sep 2024); text states conditionally accepted in Political Analysis
extraction.document_type: working paper / preprint research note (arXiv v3, dated September 6, 2024)
extraction.coverage: Full text read (127,713 chars): abstract, intro, Sec 2-4, references, Appendices A-H; figure label noise skimmed. Figure-only items (A8, H.2) not extracted. No lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation, election or turnout content; matches are legislators and text measurement. Paul markup: none (no annot_sha12s, no _annots file); p.note false. Year hint 2025 corrected to 2024 (text dated Sept 2024).
extraction.research_question: Can instruction-tuned LLMs position short texts (tweets, sentences) on ideological or policy dimensions by directly asking for a 0 to 100 score and averaging those scores to position longer texts and political actors, and how do the estimates compare with expert, crowd, roll-call, campaign-finance and classifier benchmarks?
extraction.data: (1) 899 US Congress tweets after GPT-4 cutoff (from 900 in Le Mens et al. 2023a); benchmark mean of about 20 Prolific raters per tweet (597 raters; 14,362 responses, Fig A1); tweet dates not given. (2) 98 senators (Fig 2 caption; App A.2 says 97) of the 117th Congress, 100 random tweets each; benchmark DW-NOMINATE first dimension, plus 2020 CFscore (App A8). (3) 18 British manifestos (Benoit et al. 2016), economic and social scales; expert and crowd sentence coding benchmarks. (4) 36 speeches, one European Parliament coal-subsidy debate, 10 languages; benchmark mean of six crowd codings.
extraction.method: Direct query: LLM gives a 0 to 100 JSON Score on a left-right, economic, social or pro/anti-subsidy scale, NA allowed for non-political text; temperature 0, max 20 tokens. Manifestos and speeches scored sentence by sentence and averaged. Comparators: fine-tuned BERT, GloVe and tf-idf classifiers. Validity by Pearson r with benchmarks; split-half reliability with Spearman-Brown. Robustness: dimension prompts, whole-document prompts, typicality scoring, ENO. No inference beyond correlations.
extraction.scope: US Congress members (tweets, 117th Congress senators), UK party manifestos (economic and social policy dimensions), European Parliament debate on a coal state-aid proposal in 10 languages. Era: tweets from 2023-era Congress, senators 2021-2023, manifestos from 1987-2010 labels in figures, EU debate policy horizon 2010 to 2014. Generalization is explicitly limited by the authors to the settings tested.
key_findings: Tweets (N=899, Sec 3.1, Fig 1): GPT-4o r=0.92 with crowd mean (557 scored tweets); GPT-4 r=0.90; MiXtral 8X22B 0.90; Llama 3 70Bq4 0.88; Llama 3 8B 0.80; fine-tuned BERT 0.78; tf-idf 0.66; GloVe 0.63.
Tweets within party (Fig 1): GPT-4o r=0.68 among Democratic tweets and 0.66 among Republican tweets. Text says no classifier matches the best LLMs, especially for within-party differences.

Senators of the 117th Congress (Sec 3.2, Fig 2): GPT-4o r=0.97 with first-dimension DW-NOMINATE; GPT-4 0.97; Llama 3 70Bq4 0.97; MiXtral 8X22B 0.96; Llama 3 8B 0.96; BERT 0.93; tf-idf 0.90; GloVe 0.86. Within-party GPT-4o r=0.72 (Democrats) and 0.72 (Republicans).
Senators and CFscore (App A8, figure-only): LLM positions correlate highly with 2020 campaign-finance scores overall but less so within party; coefficients are not stated in the text.

UK manifestos, economic dimension (Sec 3.3, Fig 3): GPT-4o r=0.98 overall with expert coding (Labour 0.98, Conservatives 0.33, Liberal Democrats 0.25). Crowd coding r=0.96; fine-tuned BERT 0.96; GPT-4 0.98; MiXtral 8X22B 0.97.
UK manifestos, social dimension (Fig 4): GPT-4o r=0.94 overall (Conservatives 0.79, Liberal Democrats 0.31, Labour 0.96); crowd coding 0.92; BERT 0.92; Llama 3 8B 0.88 overall with Labour only 0.46.

Whole-manifesto single prompts (App G.2, Figs A12-A13): overall economic r about 0.96 to 0.98 and social about 0.83 to 0.92, with weaker within-party fit; GPT-4 Turbo failed to return social scores for two manifestos. Authors prefer sentence-level scoring.

EU speeches in 10 languages (Sec 3.4, Fig 5): GPT-4o r=0.93 overall with six-language crowd average (Against speakers 0.91, For speakers 0.80); GPT-4 Turbo 0.86 (Against 0.07); Llama 3 70B 0.82 (Against 0.05); MiXtral 8X22B 0.78 (Against 0.04); Aya 23 35B 0.74; Llama 3 8B 0.52.

Cost and speed (Sec 4): GPT-4 API cost about 1.5 USD for the 900 tweets, versus about 1,626 pounds for the crowd coding of the same tweets; the authors note sentence-by-sentence scoring takes about one to two seconds per sentence on local models.

Non-response pattern (App E, Table A1): tweets that received an LLM score had more human ratings on average (GPT-4o 18.7) than unscored tweets (11.6), consistent with NA signaling low political content.
Effective number of observations (App E.3, Table A2): LLM scores for all tweets are worth about 3 to 7 human raters. Text says 5 to 7 for GPT-4, MiXtral and Llama 3 70B; the table lists 7 for GPT-4o.
Typicality-difference variant for tweets (App D, E.2, figure-only): correlations similar to baseline, some within-party gains, scores for all tweets.
limitations: Authors state validity is limited by the information in the input texts and that LLM estimates may differ from expert-survey positions because inputs differ.
Authors warn LLMs can be biased or unreliable in some settings and that case-by-case empirical validation remains essential before use in other domains or dimensions.
Multilingual accuracy varies by model and language, and systematic differences can bias downstream econometric analysis; authors call this an open problem.
Within-party correlations are weak for some groups (e.g. Conservative and Liberal Democrat economic positions, Labour social positions for Llama 3 8B), and the tweet within-party gap persists.
Single-prompt scoring of whole documents lowers performance for manifestos; the best single-prompt model setting for long texts is unresolved.
Training-data overlap with benchmark texts is unknown; the authors say the LLMs were most likely not trained specifically on these manifestos.
Reproducibility holds only for open models with fixed weights; API models change over time, and temperature 0 leaves residual ties and non-determinism.

Internal inconsistencies: senator N is 98 in the Fig 2 caption but 97 in App A.2; figure captions say 118th Congress for the tweets while the text says the 117th for senators; ENO values in text and Table A2 differ for GPT-4o.
Non-response (NA) is not modeled; scores are averages over only the sentences or tweets an LLM answered, which can change the composition of the average.
The paper is a research note; many robustness results (A8, H.2, Fig 5 subsets) are figure-only and not numerically reported in the text.
short_quotes: We ask an LLM where a tweet or a sentence of a political text stands on the focal dimension and take the average
This approach is generally more accurate than the positions obtained with supervised classifiers trained on large amounts of research data.
extraction.theory: No substantive theory is tested. The framing is measurement: text scaling estimates latent positions in ideological or policy spaces, and the paper builds on the direct-query typicality method of Le Mens et al. (2023a).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. Validity is established by concurrent correlation with external benchmarks (crowd ratings, expert coding, roll-call DW-NOMINATE, campaign-finance CFscore) and by comparison with supervised classifiers.
extraction.measures: Outcome: LLM Score 0 to 100 (0 = extremely left or liberal or anti-subsidy; 100 = extremely right or conservative or pro-subsidy), averaged over sentences or tweets. Benchmarks: crowd position estimate (mean of about 20 raters), expert coding, crowd-sentence coding, DW-NOMINATE first dimension, 2020 CFscore, six-language crowd mean. Metrics: Pearson r, split-half reliability with Spearman-Brown correction, ENO, mean human ratings for scored and unscored tweets, API cost.

summary_md: Le Mens and Gallego (arXiv 2311.16639, v3 dated September 2024) test a simple measurement recipe: ask an instruction-tuned LLM for a 0 to 100 position score for each short text (a tweet or one manifesto sentence), let it answer NA when the text is not on the dimension, and average the answered scores to place longer documents or actors. Across four settings the best models track human benchmarks closely. On 899 Congress tweets, GPT-4o reaches r=0.92 with a mean of about 20 crowd raters. For 117th-Congress senators, the comparison is with the first Nokken-Poole roll-call dimension, and r=0.97. On 18 UK manifestos, r=0.98 on the economic dimension and 0.94 on the social one, against expert coding. On 36 European Parliament coal-subsidy speeches in 10 languages, r=0.93 with crowd coding. Fine-tuned BERT, tf-idf and GloVe classifiers score lower. The headline figures are mostly between-party, though. Within-party correlations fall to 0.66 to 0.72 for tweets and senators. On the pro/anti-subsidy dimension, the Against group drops to 0.04 to 0.07 for every model except GPT-4o. All validity evidence is concurrent correlation, and Claude models were not tested. For Paul's systems, the paper supports using an LLM as a stance rater and contrasts with classical TF-IDF readers. It also points to three things the CU stance pipeline does not yet have: a continuous position score, explicit not-applicable handling kept separate from neutral, and validity reported within party. Because the paper's dimensions are left-right and pro/anti-subsidy, it cannot validate the target-specific credit-union stance on its own.

extraction.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
extraction.venue: Queen's Economics Department Working Paper 1314 (reissued and corrected 2019-08); published as Journal of Applied Econometrics 32 (2017) 233-254
extraction.document_type: working paper (Monte Carlo and placebo-law simulation study with one empirical replication; published journal version exists)
extraction.coverage: Full text read (3813 lines): front matter, Sections 1-9, references, Appendix A.1-A.8 with captions. Text only, so figure curves were not visible. Paul markup: none (no annotation file), nothing dropped. Corrected 2019-08 reissue. Relevance: no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation, election, persuasion, legislator or text-measurement content; closest is cluster inference for state-level policy treatments (Sections 5, 7, 8).
extraction.research_question: When is inference with cluster robust variance estimator t statistics (CRVE, with t(G-1) critical values) reliable, and which alternatives (effective number of clusters G* critical values, restricted or unrestricted wild cluster bootstrap) work when cluster sizes are very unequal or the number of treated clusters is small?
extraction.theory: Asymptotic validity of the CRVE under White (1984) assumptions A1 (number of clusters grows), A2 (same within-cluster error correlation) and A3 (equal cluster sizes). Wild cluster bootstrap with Rademacher weights (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2008; Webb 2014 for G below about 12). Effective number of clusters G* of Carter, Schnepel and Steigerwald (2017). Section 6 analytic argument: with G1 fixed, the treatment coefficient is inconsistent, and the variance of the residual sum for a treated cluster shrinks by the factor (M1 minus N1) over M1 under IID errors (eq. A.2).
extraction.identification: Not a causal identification paper. Test size is the object: the null beta equal to zero holds in the simulations and placebo laws, and the question is whether CRVE t tests and bootstrap P values have correct size when cluster sizes are unequal and the number of treated clusters is small.
extraction.data: Monte Carlo (Sections 4-6, Appendix A.2, A.6): simulated samples of N = 2000 observations (G = 50 or 100 clusters, equal sizes or sizes proportional to U.S. state populations without DC; smallest state cluster 4 obs and largest 242 for G = 50; 400,000 replications; 399 bootstrap draws). Appendix A.6 uses N = 50G with G = 12, 16, 20, 25, 32. Placebo laws (Section 7): U.S. Current Population Survey, women aged 25-50, 1979-1999, log weekly earnings, earnings under 20 dollars dropped, 547,518 micro observations, 51 states including DC, year of treatment start 1985-1995; 100,000 or 10,000 replications; G* computed on a 1/100 subsample; rho-hat about 0.031-0.032. Aggregate version: 1071 state-year cells of 21 obs each. Empirical example (Section 8): Angrist and Kugler (2008) Colombia, men 181,882 obs in 32 departments (aggregate 288 dept-year cells); teenage boys 22,141 obs in 38 departments (aggregate 340 cells); 99,999 bootstrap samples.
extraction.method: Monte Carlo rejection frequencies at nominal .05 (and .10 and .01 in places) for: CRVE t with t(N-2), t(G-1), t(G*-1) and t(G*) critical values (G* at rho = 0.99 and rho-hat); restricted wild cluster bootstrap (WCR) with symmetric P values; unrestricted bootstrap (WCU, Appendix A.3); HCCME t with normal critical values. Rho-hat from the cluster-dummy regression. Power comparison of micro versus aggregate estimators (Appendix A.8) with bootstrap tests.
extraction.scope: Inference in linear models with clustered errors, with a focus on U.S. state-level clusters. Simulation designs are synthetic; placebo-law and empirical examples use CPS 1979-1999 earnings and Colombian household data from 1995-2000. Results are for G from 12 to 200 clusters and at most 2000 observations in the main Monte Carlo designs.
key_findings: Section 4, Table 1 (p.6): with 50 equal-sized clusters, t(G-1) rejection rises with the regressor's within-cluster correlation and exceeds 0.065 when rho_x is 1 (value 0.06568 at rho_eps 0). Wild bootstrap rejections in Tables 1 and 3 all lie close to .05 (Table 1 range 0.04924 to 0.05084, p.8).

Section 4, Table 2 (p.7): with 50 state-sized clusters (sizes 4 to 242), t(G-1) rejection is 0.05784 with both correlations zero and reaches 0.10718 at rho_eps 0.9 and rho_x 1 (text says 0.1073, a small mismatch with the table). Bootstrap rejections range 0.04905 to 0.05277 (p.10).

Section 4 (p.10): with state-sized clusters, t(G*-1) critical values underreject severely when rho_x is large; worst case rejection 0.0166 at rho_eps 0 and rho_x 0.6, where average G* is 9.43 using rho-hat and 5.97 using rho 0.99.

Section 4, Table 4 (p.9): with 100 state-sized clusters (each state appearing twice), t(G-1) rejection reaches 0.08442 (rho_eps 0.9, rho_x 1); the wild cluster bootstrap never exceeds 0.05124. The rule of 42 fails under unequal clusters even at 100 clusters.

Section 5, Figure 1 (p.11): for DiD with t(G-1) critical values, severe overrejection when G1 (treated clusters) or G minus G1 is near 0; with equal-sized clusters rejection is near .05 for G1 from 17 to 34. Overrejection is worse when the smallest clusters are treated first.

Section 5, Figure 2 (p.12): t(G*-1) critical values overreject except when the number of treated clusters is very small or very large; extreme underrejection at G1 = 1 and G1 = 49. Figure 3 (p.13): restricted wild bootstrap underrejects severely when G1 or G minus G1 is very small but works extremely well for G1 from about 7 to 43 (equal-sized clusters).

Section 6 (pp.16-17, Figure 4): with G1 = 1 and 50 equal clusters, the 0.975 quantile of the CRVE t statistic is 14.226 versus 2.010 for t(49); the t(G-1) test rejects 77.75 percent of the time at .05; restricted wild bootstrap tests never reject at conventional levels when G1 = 1 in the experiments.

Section 6 (p.19): for DiD with equal-sized clusters, the wild cluster bootstrap (restricted or unrestricted) can probably be used safely for 7 <= G1 <= G-7; likely misleading below 4 or above G-4. Appendix A.6 (p.39): with unbalanced clusters and G of 20 or 32, the restricted bootstrap is acceptable for 6 <= G1 <= G-5. Exact cutoffs are data dependent.

Section 7 (pp.21-23): placebo laws with micro CPS data; HCCME t tests reject more than 50 percent of the time at .05 for all G1; t(G-1) CRVE rejects at least 0.063 whenever many states are treated and about 0.07 half the time, with severe overrejection when few states are treated; restricted bootstrap underrejects severely when G1 is very small but performs extremely well for larger G1 (Figure 9).

Section 7 (p.24, Figure 10): with aggregated state-year data (balanced cells), CRVE t(G-1) performs very well for most G1 and slightly underrejects; restricted wild bootstrap performs extremely well for G1 at least 5. Appendix A.7 reports unrestricted bootstrap rejection 0.7184 at .05 for G1 = 1 with aggregate data.

Section 8, Table 5 Panel A (p.27): adult men (32 departments, N = 181,882), rural 1998-2000 coefficient 0.1219 with s.e. 0.0359 (t = 3.395); t(G-1) p = 0.002, bootstrap p = 0.028, t(G*-1) p = 0.059 with G* = 3.402. Rural 1995-1997 has t(G-1) p = 0.045 but bootstrap p = 0.186. Only the rural 1998-2000 term is significant at .05 under the bootstrap.

Section 8, Table 5 Panel B (p.27): teenage boys (38 departments, N = 22,141), rho-hat 0.155, G* between 8.9 and 12.9; both rural coefficients significant under t(G-1) (p 0.028 and 0.048) and bootstrap (p 0.030 and 0.050), but t(G*-1) p-values are 0.051 and 0.067. Urban coefficients have p of at least 0.6.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: placebo-law G* uses a 1/100 subsample; Bell-McCaffrey and Imbens-Kolesar corrections not studied; Ibragimov-Muller does not apply to most designs; Rademacher weights not recommended below about 12 clusters. Bootstrap reliability depends on G1 with no clean cutoff, and heteroskedasticity by treatment status could change results. G* depends sharply on rho. No G* for joint tests. Pure-treatment results changed after a rho correction (Appendix A.2), unexplained.
short_quotes: we show that the rule of 42 no longer holds when the assumption of equal-sized clusters is relaxed (Section 1, p.2)
the wild cluster bootstrap procedure always performs extremely well (Section 1, p.3)
this procedure fails when a small number of clusters is treated (Abstract, p.1)
extraction.measures: Rejection frequency at nominal .05; cluster robust t statistic; effective number of clusters G* (depends on rho); treated clusters G1 and treated observations M1; ratio N1 over M1 for the largest treated cluster; rho-hat from cluster dummies; HCCME standard error; symmetric bootstrap P value.

summary_md: MacKinnon and Webb (Queen's WP 1314, corrected 2019; JAE 2017) study when cluster-robust (CRVE) t tests with t(G-1) critical values give correct size, and when the wild cluster bootstrap does better. Using Monte Carlo designs with 50 or 100 clusters sized like U.S. states (4 to 242 observations), CPS placebo laws (547,518 obs, 51 states) and a Colombian replication, they show the rule of 42 fails once cluster sizes are unequal: t(G-1) rejects up to 0.107 at nominal .05 with 50 state-sized clusters and 0.084 even with 100. The restricted wild cluster bootstrap (WCR) stays near .05 in those designs (0.049 to 0.053). The bootstrap breaks when few clusters are treated: with one treated cluster of 50 the t(G-1) test rejects 77.75 percent of the time while the WCR never rejects; WCR is safe roughly for 7 <= G1 <= G-7 with equal clusters and 6 <= G1 <= G-5 with unbalanced clusters at G of 20 to 32. The effective-clusters G* correction is erratic. Rademacher weights are not advised below about 12 clusters. For Paul's systems the paper is the method source for one component: the Mentat sector growth study already runs a WCR bootstrap-t by sector with Webb six-point weights, enumerating all 6^G draws when small, and labels per-sector terms resting on one cluster DESCRIPTIVE, which matches the paper's G1 = 1 warning. The open point is scale: the study runs with 3 to 9 sector clusters, below the 12-cluster floor of every design the paper tests, so the paper supports the procedure choice but does not certify its size at G = 9 or 5. No network, lobbying-edge or influence claim follows.

bearings.paper_claim: With unequal state-sized clusters (G = 50, Table 2) CRVE t(G-1) rejection at nominal .05 runs from 0.0567 to 0.1078 across the rho grid (0.10718 at rho_eps 0.9, rho_x 1); at G = 100 (Table 4) it reaches 0.08442; the restricted wild cluster bootstrap stays between 0.04905 and 0.05277 (Table 2). The conclusion recommends WCR over t(G-1) and says G* critical values often improve matters but do not always work as well.

Clusters are sectors for sector-year tests but champions (bioguide) for the H5 tests, so the analyst's sector-only system_side is overbroad.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's size evidence is for Rademacher weights. The study uses Webb six-point weights, which this paper does not evaluate; it only cites Webb (2014) for G below about 12. Paper designs are linear models with G from 12 to 200. Whether the study's sector cluster sizes are near-balanced was not checked against study data in this pass; H5 bioguide clusters are the likely unequal-size case.

The sector-only clustering claim fails for H5 per the config comment. The paper evaluates Rademacher weights only, so support for the Webb six-point choice is not established by this paper.

extraction.research_question: Do members of Congress who exchange senior or policy staff across offices become more similar in legislative effectiveness and in roll-call ideology than chance or observed covariates would predict? Secondary: do staff ties transmit expertise and positions across legislators, as opposed to homophily in staff hiring?
extraction.theory: Staff are not mere extensions of members (p.3-4). Two mechanisms (p.7-8): (1) a staffer carries knowledge, relationships with party leaders and expertise from a prior boss to a new boss; (2) staff who move between offices facilitate coordination between the two offices. Hypothesis 1: linked offices are more similar in legislative effectiveness. Hypothesis 2: linked offices vote more similarly. Senior staff are expected to matter for effectiveness; policy staff for roll-call voting (p.9).
extraction.data: CQ First Street personal-staff records for House members, digitized from CQ Press directories 1993-2009 and updated after (p.10). Subset to personal staff, 103rd-111th Congresses; staff ties built for the 105th-111th Congresses. Unit: member-Congress. 3,973 member-Congress observations in the period; staff data missing for 112 (2.8%) (p.11). Regression N per Congress 435-446 (Tables 1-4). Outcomes: Volden and Wiseman (2014) legislative effectiveness scores (LES, range 0-18.7, mean 0.996, SD 1.526 in the 105th-111th); Bayesian one-dimensional ideal points from Clinton, Jackman and Rivers (2004), estimated with pscl on Voteview roll calls (Online Appendix). Committee staff excluded because majority/minority status and member links are unreliable (p.31; Online Appendix). Descriptives: 12 percent of senior/policy staff held such a post for two or more House members, 44 percent among those serving five or more Congresses (p.13); fewer than 50 of 12,938 senior/policy staffers crossed party lines (p.14).
extraction.method: Bayesian heteroskedastic spatial autoregressive model with covariates, y = X beta + rho W y + e, with e having variance sigma^2 V (diagonal scalars, Student-t-like errors, r = 4), estimated in Matlab with sar_g (LeSage and Pace 2009) (p.17-18). W is a row-standardized, symmetric count of staff who worked for both members in the current or previous two Congresses (p.18). Separate cross-sectional model per Congress, pooled across Congresses with the Gelman et al. (2004) procedure because W changes over time (p.19). Direct, total and indirect effects from the (I - rho W)^-1 expansion (p.20). Two networks: senior-only ties and senior-plus-policy ties. Controls: seniority, majority party, female, African American, Hispanic, committee chair, subchair, majority and minority leadership, power committee (LES); Democrat, female, race and ethnicity, district presidential vote and its square (ideology). Falsification: placebo ties from lower-level staff and from future senior ties (p.29-30).
extraction.identification: Observational. Identification rests on the spatial lag rho capturing outcome similarity among members linked by staff moves, net of covariates. No design isolates an exogenous staff shock. Falsification tests are used to probe homophily: lower-level staff ties and future senior ties, which should not causally matter (p.29-30). The authors state homophily cannot be fully ruled out (p.30). Causal language for race is acknowledged as problematic (p.28, footnote 34).
extraction.scope: U.S. House only; personal senior and policy staff only; committee staff excluded; 105th-111th Congresses (roughly 1997-2010 by calendar arithmetic; text does not give years for these Congresses). Explicitly does not test the 1970s-era 'textbook Congress' (p.31).
extraction.measures: Staff tie weight: count of shared senior or policy staffers across current and previous two Congresses, row-standardized (p.18). Senior staff: chief of staff, director variants, administrative assistant variants; policy staff: legislative assistant, counsel, issue specialists (p.4 note 2; Online Appendix keyword lists). LES from Volden and Wiseman (2014); ideology from Clinton, Jackman and Rivers (2004); district vote from Jacobson data (Online Appendix).
key_findings: Senior-staff ties, LES: pooled rho = 0.043, 95% CI [0.0095, 0.096]; positive in 5 of 7 Congresses but not each reliably above zero (Table 1, p.22-23).
Senior plus policy ties, LES: pooled rho = 0.013, 95% CI [-0.015, 0.037]; authors call it consistent with expectations but not conclusive (Table 2, p.24).
Senior-staff ties, ideology: pooled rho = -0.003, 95% CI [-0.029, 0.020]; no reliable effect on roll-call ideal points (Table 3, p.26).
Senior plus policy ties, ideology: pooled rho = 0.028, 95% CI [0.0129, 0.0465]; reliably positive in the 109th and 110th Congresses per text (Table 4, p.27).
Ideology R2 above 0.88 in every Congress, so the tie effect is small against the covariates (p.27-28).
Committee chair direct effect on LES 1.853, 90% CI [1.376, 2.352]; indirect effect via ties 0.442, 90% CI [0.131, 0.826] (p.24).
Being African American, 109th Congress ideology: direct effect 0.176, 90% CI [0.042, 0.317]; indirect effect via ties 0.0093, 90% CI [0.0003, 0.0238] (p.28).
Falsification, lower-level staff ties on LES: pooled rho about -0.016; text gives CI [-0.070, 0.027], which excludes the 0.043 headline point (Table 5 p.30; text p.29).
Falsification, future senior ties on LES: pooled CI [-0.033, 0.071] overlaps the headline estimate, so homophily cannot be excluded (p.29).
Falsification, lower-level ties on ideology: pooled 0.006, CI [-0.016, 0.067] overlaps the Table 4 estimate (p.29).

Robustness (Online Appendix Table A1): no-covariate and committee-fixed-effects models keep the LES pattern for senior ties; two-Congress window leaves the senior LES interval barely including zero (-0.0006, 0.1088).
Authors conclude staff may act as extensions of members (Kingdon 1973) and that the ideology link is partly homophily (p.30-31).
limitations: Cannot test long-term changes in staff roles or the textbook Congress era (p.31).
House only; Senate not studied (p.31).
Committee staff excluded; their effects untested (p.31; Online Appendix).
Imperfect outcome measures, LES and ideal points (p.31).
No multiplex analysis with cosponsorship or other dyadic ties (p.31).
Homophily between staff and members not fully ruled out; future designs needed (p.31).
Staff missing for 2.8 percent of observations, and some members repeatedly fail to match (Online Appendix).
Covariate choice affects inference; committee dummies removed power committee for collinearity (Online Appendix).

summary_md: Montgomery and Nyhan ask whether House members linked by shared personal staff become alike in legislative effectiveness (Volden-Wiseman LES) and roll-call ideology (CJR ideal points). A tie between two members is the count of senior or policy staffers who worked for both offices in the current or previous two Congresses, row-standardized, over the 105th-111th Congresses (435-446 members per Congress). They fit a Bayesian heteroskedastic spatial autoregressive model per Congress and pool the seven estimates. Senior-staff ties show a small positive LES lag (pooled rho 0.043, 95% CI 0.0095 to 0.096; positive in 5 of 7 Congresses). Adding policy staff weakens it (0.013, CI -0.015 to 0.037). For ideology, senior ties show nothing (-0.003). Senior plus policy ties show a small positive lag (0.028, CI 0.013 to 0.047), but covariates already explain R2 above 0.88. Placebo tests help only partly. Lower-level staff ties give a null LES lag. Future senior ties (CI -0.033 to 0.071) and the lower-level ideology placebo overlap the headline estimates, so homophily is not ruled out. The authors conclude that staff may act as extensions of their members. For Paul's systems the paper is most useful as a comparison for the staffer network. Montgomery's tie is an office-to-office sequence link, which the system already emits as directed office moves and shared_with counts. The system deliberately does not treat that link as a person-to-person edge. In this paper the link carries only a weak signal of similarity, and the signal is partly confounded by homophily. It supports showing these counts as descriptive data. It does not support treating them as transmission channels. All findings are observational and House-only. The window is 1997-2010 and excludes committee staff.

summary_issues: Calls Montgomery's tie an office-to-office sequence link that the system emits as directed moves. The paper's W is an undirected, row-standardized co-service count over the current and two prior Congresses (p.11, fn 12, p.18). Sequence is the theory, not the operational tie.
States the window as 1997-2010. The text gives only the 105th-111th Congresses and never states years; 1997-2010 is calendar arithmetic.

Says the senior ideology result shows nothing (-0.003). Strictly, the paper says only that it is not reliably distinguishable from zero (95% CI -0.029 to 0.020); Table 3 has 4 of 7 Congress estimates positive, so the summary's flat reading is a fair shorthand but not a finding of no effect.
gaps_exposed: No member-level staff-sharing measure matches the paper's specification (senior/policy titles only, current plus two prior Congresses, row-standardized). shared_with counts every shared person with no window, so a published-style replication on the system's payroll data is not possible as shipped.
No check exists for homophily versus transmission on staff-move links (for example, a future-ties placebo). Any use of office_moves beyond description lacks a falsification design.
Committee staff are excluded in the paper, but the system's co-tenure layer gives committee containers kappa 0.75/0.60/0.40. No literature here addresses committee-staff ties.
The paper does not test multiplex combination with cosponsorship (its own limitation, p.31). Whether staff-move ties add information beyond the cosponsor kernel edges is untested in the system.
flags: Causal wording (effects, indirect effects transmitted through ties) outruns the design. Placebos do not exclude homophily (p.29-31). If cited in Melange, staff-sharing ties must not be described as influence, access or introduction channels (D-025). The paper's figures are similarity estimates on 1997-2010 House data.
Pooled rho values pool seven per-Congress estimates spanning a majority flip (110th). Quote them with the per-Congress strata in Tables 1-4, not as a single pooled coefficient.

The source text is internally inconsistent. p.19 says 105th to 112th Congress while the data end at the 111th. p.27 calls the 110th ideology rho reliably positive, but Table 4 gives 0.024 (SE 0.021). The lower-level ideology placebo point 0.006 sits oddly inside its interval [-0.016, 0.067].
The row-standardized W is a SAR convention (per-row normalization), not the rejected per-edge volume normalization. The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal.

The paper cites Drutman 2012 and Bertrand et al. 2014 on staff becoming lobbyists but does not analyze revolving-door edges. Nothing here licenses influence language on revolving-door edges or the use of LDA as an edge source (D-021).
paul_alignment: No Paul entry for this work. His staffer position (staffers as gatekeepers, professional ties as conduits) is tempered here. Shared senior staff predict only small LES similarity, ideology barely moves beyond covariates, and homophily is not excluded. The system as built agrees: sequence stays an office-move property, never a person-person edge, and shared-staff counts are descriptive. His overlap note is not stale; this paper adds the empirical reason sequence links should stay descriptive.
